steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on robust fidelity metrics for evaluating GNN explanations. It should explain why GNN explainability matters, how explanations are currently evaluated with fidelity metrics, why those metrics break under distribution shift, and summarize our information-theoretic framework and contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- GNNs: widespread success, need to understand their decisions; subgraph-based explanations
- Evaluation metrics matter: ground truth rare, fidelity metrics (Fid_{+}, Fid_{-}) as surrogates
- Problem: explanation / non-explanation subgraphs are OOD for the model (MUTAG example)
- Challenges for robust fidelity evaluation
- Our information-theoretic framework and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- GNNs
  - cornerstone for graph-structured data; node classification, link prediction (cite)
  - used in sensitive sectors (healthcare, fraud detection) -> demand for understanding decisions (cite)
  - explanation techniques: mostly identify subgraph dominating the prediction, post-hoc (cite)
- Evaluation metrics
  - both model design and evaluation metrics matter; most work on new architectures/objectives (cite)
  - this paper: importance of choosing the right evaluation metrics
  - ideal: compare with ground truth explanation (cite); rare in real-world applications
  - surrogate fidelity metrics Fid_{+}, Fid_{-}, Fid_{\Delta} for faithfulness
  - intuition: discriminative subgraph removed -> prediction changes a lot; otherwise maintained
  - Fid_{+}: accuracy/probability difference, original vs. non-explanation subgraph (explanation masked out) (cite); Fid_{-}: original vs. explanation subgraph (cite)
  - used in platforms: GraphFramEx, GraphXAI, GNNX-BENCH, DIG (cite each)
- Drawbacks
  - assumes model predicts accurately on explanation subgraph (Fid_{-}) / non-explanation subgraph (Fid_{+})
  - removing edges -> subgraphs may be OOD (cite)
  - MUTAG (cite): molecules, nodes = atoms, edges = chemical bonds; NO_{2} group -> mutagenic; explanation only 2 edges, much smaller than molecule
  - distribution shift violates training/test same distribution assumption (cite)
- Challenges
  - goal: robust fidelity for correctness of explanations, evaluation foundation for XAI on graphs
  - GNN is black-box, cannot be re-trained for generalization (cite)
  - evaluation must be stable, ideally deterministic; parametric methods e.g. adversarial perturbations (cite) unsuitable, random initialization
- Framework and contributions
  - explanation graph = subgraph that is (almost) sufficient statistic for output label + small vs. input graph
  - two notions: explainability of a classification task and of a classifier (Definitions 2 and 3); relation for low-error classifiers (Theorem 1)
  - exact measure needs graph statistics, impossible in practice -> generalized class of surrogate fidelity measures robust to distribution shift (Proposition A.4)
  - contributions: spotlight shortcomings of accepted evaluation; new metrics resilient to distribution shift, closer to ground-truth evaluations; empirical validation on synthetic + real datasets

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a cornerstone for processing data that is structured as graphs, and they achieve impressive results in many domains like node classification and link prediction. However, as they spread into sensitive sectors like healthcare and fraud detection, there is a much bigger demand to understand how they make decisions. To deal with this, explanation techniques for GNNs have been proposed, and most of them focus on finding a subgraph that dominates the prediction of the model, in a post-hoc way.

When designing and studying explainable GNNs, both the design of the model and the choice of evaluation metrics are important. Most efforts so far went into developing new network architectures and optimization objectives to get more accurate explanations, but in this paper we stress how important it is to choose the right evaluation metrics for the explanations. Ideally, an explanation subgraph can be evaluated quantitatively by comparing it with a gold standard or ground truth explanation. But in real-world applications such ground truth explanation subgraphs are rare, which often makes direct comparison impossible. Instead, surrogate fidelity metrics, namely Fid_{+}, Fid_{-}, and Fid_{\Delta}, are used to measure how faithful explanation subgraphs are. The intuition behind these fidelity metrics is simple: if a subgraph is discriminative to the model, the prediction should change a lot when the subgraph is removed from the input. If not, the prediction should stay the same. So Fid_{+} is defined as the difference in accuracy (or predicted probability) between the original prediction and the new prediction on the non-explanation subgraph, which we get by masking out the explanation subgraph, and Fid_{-} measures the difference between the predictions on the original graph and on the explanation subgraph. These Fidelity metrics and their variants are the current standard and are widely used in popular platforms, such as GraphFramEx, GraphXAI, GNNX-BENCH, and DIG.

These Fidelity metrics are intuitively correct, but we argue that they have significant drawbacks, because they make the impractical assumption that the model being explained can make accurate predictions on the explanation subgraph (in Fid_{-}) or the non-explanation subgraph (in Fid_{+}). This is not true in a lot of real-world scenarios, because when edges are removed the resulting subgraphs can be Out Of Distribution (OOD). For example, in the MUTAG dataset, each graph is a molecule, the nodes are atoms and the edges are the chemical bonds. The functional group NO_{2} is considered the dominating subgraph that makes a molecule mutagenic. The explanation subgraph only has 2 edges, which is much smaller than the whole molecular graphs. Such differences in properties cause distribution shifts, and this puts the Fidelity metrics on shaky ground, because a key assumption in machine learning is violated, that the training and test data come from the same distribution.

- Challenges:
  - robust fidelity for correctness of explanations; foundation for XAI on graphs
  - black-box GNN, cannot be re-trained for generalization
  - evaluation must be stable/deterministic; adversarial perturbations unsuitable (random initial parameters)
- Framework:
  - explanation graph = (almost) sufficient statistic of input graph w.r.t. label, and small
  - explainability of classification task vs. of classifier (Definitions 2 and 3); relation for low-error classifiers (Theorem 1)
  - needs unknown graph statistics -> generalized surrogate fidelity measures robust to distribution shift (Proposition A.4)
- Contributions:
  - shortcomings of accepted evaluation methods
  - new metrics resilient to distribution shifts, closer to ground truth evaluations
  - experiments on synthetic and real datasets agree with gold standard

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a cornerstone for processing data that is structured as graphs, and they achieve impressive results in many domains like node classification and link prediction. However, as they spread into sensitive sectors like healthcare and fraud detection, there is a much bigger demand to understand how they make decisions. To deal with this, explanation techniques for GNNs have been proposed, and most of them focus on finding a subgraph that dominates the prediction of the model, in a post-hoc way.

When designing and studying explainable GNNs, both the design of the model and the choice of evaluation metrics are important. Most efforts so far went into developing new network architectures and optimization objectives to get more accurate explanations, but in this paper we stress how important it is to choose the right evaluation metrics for the explanations. Ideally, an explanation subgraph can be evaluated quantitatively by comparing it with a gold standard or ground truth explanation. But in real-world applications such ground truth explanation subgraphs are rare, which often makes direct comparison impossible. Instead, surrogate fidelity metrics, namely Fid_{+}, Fid_{-}, and Fid_{\Delta}, are used to measure how faithful explanation subgraphs are. The intuition behind these fidelity metrics is simple: if a subgraph is discriminative to the model, the prediction should change a lot when the subgraph is removed from the input. If not, the prediction should stay the same. So Fid_{+} is defined as the difference in accuracy (or predicted probability) between the original prediction and the new prediction on the non-explanation subgraph, which we get by masking out the explanation subgraph, and Fid_{-} measures the difference between the predictions on the original graph and on the explanation subgraph. These Fidelity metrics and their variants are the current standard and are widely used in popular platforms, such as GraphFramEx, GraphXAI, GNNX-BENCH, and DIG.

These Fidelity metrics are intuitively correct, but we argue that they have significant drawbacks, because they make the impractical assumption that the model being explained can make accurate predictions on the explanation subgraph (in Fid_{-}) or the non-explanation subgraph (in Fid_{+}). This is not true in a lot of real-world scenarios, because when edges are removed the resulting subgraphs can be Out Of Distribution (OOD). For example, in the MUTAG dataset, each graph is a molecule, the nodes are atoms and the edges are the chemical bonds. The functional group NO_{2} is considered the dominating subgraph that makes a molecule mutagenic. The explanation subgraph only has 2 edges, which is much smaller than the whole molecular graphs. Such differences in properties cause distribution shifts, and this puts the Fidelity metrics on shaky ground, because a key assumption in machine learning is violated, that the training and test data come from the same distribution.

In this paper we investigate robust fidelity measurements for evaluating the correctness of explanations, in order to build an evaluation foundation for eXplainable AI (XAI) in the graph domain. This problem has several non-trivial challenges. First, the GNN model to be explained is usually treated as a black-box model, so it cannot be re-trained to make sure it generalizes. Second, the evaluation method needs to be stable and ideally deterministic. So complex parametric methods, like adversarial perturbations, do not fit, because their results depend on randomly initialized parameters.

We give an information theoretic framework for GNN explainability. We define an explanation graph as a subgraph of the input that meets two conditions: 1) the explanation graph is an (almost) sufficient statistic of the input graph with respect to the output label, and 2) the explanation graph is small compared to the input graph. Based on this, we give two notions of explainability, the explainability of a classification task and the explainability of a classifier for that task (Definitions 2 and 3). We quantify how these two notions relate for low-error classifiers and classification tasks (Theorem 1). To compute the resulting information theoretic fidelity measure we would need to know the underlying graph statistics, which is not possible in most real-world scenarios we care about. So we propose a generalized class of surrogate fidelity measures that are robust to distribution shift issues in many scenarios (Proposition A.4). Our contributions are as follows.

- We are the first to point out the inherent shortcomings of the widely accepted evaluation methods in the explainable graph learning domain.

- Based on solid theory, we introduce new evaluation metrics that are resilient to distribution shifts, which makes them more applicable in real-world settings. This metric also approximates evaluations done with ground truth explanations more closely.

- With rigorous empirical analysis on a diverse mix of synthetic and real datasets, we validate that our approach agrees well with gold standard benchmarks.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a cornerstone for processing graph-structured data, achieving impressive results across various domains such as node classification and link prediction [1,2,3,4]. However, with their spread into sensitive sectors like healthcare and fraud detection, the demand for understanding their decision-making processes has grown significantly [5,6,7]. To address this challenge, explanation techniques have been proposed for GNNs, most commonly focusing on identifying a subgraph that dominates the model's prediction in a post-hoc way [8,9,10].

In the design and study of explainable GNNs, both model design and the choice of evaluation metrics are important. While most efforts have been made to develop new network architectures and optimization objectives to achieve more accurate explanations [8,9,10], in this paper we underscore the critical importance of choosing the right evaluation metrics for the resulting explanations. Ideally, quantitative evaluation of an explanation subgraph can be done by comparing it with a gold standard or ground truth explanation [8]. Yet in real-world applications such ground truth explanation subgraphs are rare, which often makes direct comparisons impracticable. Instead, surrogate fidelity metrics, namely Fid_{+}, Fid_{-}, and Fid_{\Delta}, have been used to gauge the faithfulness of explanation subgraphs. The intuition behind such fidelity metrics is straightforward: if a subgraph is discriminative to the model, the prediction should change significantly when it is removed from the input; otherwise, the prediction should be maintained. Hence, Fid_{+} is defined as the difference in accuracy (or predicted probability) between the original prediction and the new prediction of the non-explanation subgraph, which is obtained by masking out the explanation subgraph [11,12], and Fid_{-} measures the difference between the predictions of the original graph and the explanation subgraph [13]. As prevailing standards, these Fidelity metrics and their variants are widely used in existing popular platforms, such as GraphFramEx [14], GraphXAI [15], GNNX-BENCH [16], and DIG [17].

Although intuitively correct, we argue that these Fidelity metrics have significant drawbacks, due to the impractical assumption that the model to be explained can make accurate predictions of the explanation subgraph (in Fid_{-}) or the non-explanation subgraph (in Fid_{+}). This does not hold in many real-world scenarios, because when edges are removed, the resulting subgraphs might be Out Of Distribution (OOD) [18,19]. For example, in the MUTAG dataset [20], each graph is a molecule with nodes representing atoms and edges describing the chemical bonds. The functional group NO_{2} is considered the dominating subgraph that causes a molecule to be mutagenic. The explanation subgraph consists of only 2 edges, which is much smaller than the whole molecular graphs. Such differences in properties introduce distribution shifts, putting the Fidelity metrics on shaky ground, because they violate a key assumption in machine learning: that the training and test data come from the same distribution [21].

To build an evaluation foundation for eXplainable AI (XAI) in the graph domain, in this paper we investigate robust fidelity measurements for evaluating the correctness of explanations. There are several non-trivial challenges associated with this problem. First, the GNN model to be explained is usually evaluated as a black-box model, which cannot be re-trained to ensure its generalization capacity [21]. Second, the evaluation method needs to be stable and ideally deterministic. As a result, complex parametric methods, such as adversarial perturbations [22,23], are not suitable, as their results are affected by randomly initialized parameters.

We provide an information theoretic framework for GNN explainability. We define an explanation graph as a subgraph of the input that satisfies two conditions: 1) the explanation graph is an (almost) sufficient statistic of the input graph with respect to the output label, and 2) the explanation graph is small compared to the input graph. Based on this, we provide two notions of explainability: explainability of a classification task and explainability of a classifier for the task (Definitions 2 and 3). We quantify the relation between these two notions for low-error classifiers and classification tasks (Theorem 1). Computing the resulting information theoretic fidelity measure requires knowledge of the underlying graph statistics, which is not possible in most real-world scenarios of interest. We therefore propose a generalized class of surrogate fidelity measures that are robust to distribution shift issues in a wide range of scenarios (Proposition A.4). Our contributions are summarized as follows.

- We are the first to spotlight the inherent shortcomings of widely accepted evaluation methodologies in the explainable graph learning domain.

- Grounded in solid theory, we introduce novel evaluation metrics that are resilient to distribution shifts, enhancing their applicability in real-world settings. This metric also approximates evaluations conducted with ground truth explanations more closely.

- Through rigorous empirical analyses on a diverse mix of synthetic and real datasets, we validate that our approach agrees well with gold standard benchmarks.
